idiom_name: spool file per message (write + fsync + rename) drained by a poll loop
implementation_notes: The local store is the filesystem: write each message to a temporary file in the spool directory, fsync() it, rename() it to its final name so it appears atomically to the drainer, and fsync() the directory as well - fsync(2) documents that a file's own fsync does not cover the directory entry, so without the second call the rename can be lost in a crash. The forwarder is an ordinary loop (optionally woken by poll(2)/epoll on an eventfd) that walks the spool in name order, delivers, and unlinks only after the peer acknowledged. POSIX message queues are not the store: mq_overview(7) grants them kernel persistence only, so the queue and its messages are gone when the system shuts down. A broker client or this hand-written loop both replace the 'send and hope' call; the classic structure is justified exactly when there is no messaging runtime and accepted work must outlive the process.
pitfalls: fsync() on the file does not persist the directory entry; without the directory fsync the rename can be lost, leaving a missing or empty spool entry after a crash.
rename() is only atomic within one filesystem - renaming across devices fails with EXDEV, so the temporary file must be created in the spool directory itself.
write() may write fewer bytes than requested and can be interrupted (EINTR); loop until the buffer is consumed and treat short writes as errors.
POSIX message queues (mq_open/mq_send) look like a local queue but only have kernel persistence, so they cannot hold the backlog across a shutdown.
